header: Date: 2026-12-01 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 60 mins | Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood), Maya Patel (Aurelius CTO), Ethan Ross (Aurelius Infra), Sofia García (Aurelius Security)
summary: Technical deep dive on Private VPC deployment for Aurelius Financial. Main focus: networking topology (PrivateLink vs NAT vs VPC peering), DNS strategies (split-horizon, Route53 inbound/outbound endpoints), runtime implications for latency/throughput, KV cache and batching tradeoffs, quantization impact on memory/latency, and security integrations (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Action items agreed for network artifact exchange and benchmark runs.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um today we wanted to run through the private VPC setup and then dig into runtime perf implications, so Priya will lead the networking and I'll chime on security/pricing.
[00:12] Maya: Thanks Jordan, we have Maya here and Ethan and Sofia from infra/security. we're evaluating dedicated vs private VPC and mostly concerned about latency and auditability.
[00:22] Priya: Great, quick agenda — private link / interface endpoints, NAT egress vs PrivateLink, route tables, split-horizon DNS, and then runtime: KV cache placement, batching behavior across AZs, quantization memory footprints.
[00:35] Ethan: A couple constraints up front: our VPC is locked down, no internet egress except via our NAT gateway, and we have strict egress auditing. Also everything has to go through the corp proxy for certain endpoints.
[00:46] Jordan: Got it. so two high level options: Redwood Private with PrivateLink (interface endpoints in customer VPC that connect to Redwood's NLB via AWS PrivateLink) or host in your VPC where we'd run the runtime inside customer-managed infra. Each has different tradeoffs on latency and ops.
[01:05] Priya: If we do PrivateLink, traffic goes over the AWS backbone and you avoid hairpin NAT and public internet hops; typically that reduces tail latency, but you still have an extra ENI and interface endpoint in each AZ which has cost. Also DNS for PrivateLink endpoints — you either use AWS-provided DNS or create a private hosted zone with records pointing to the interface endpoint.
[01:25] Sofia: When you say DNS — is that split-horizon? we need internal names not resolvable publicly.
[01:29] Priya: Yep, split-horizon is common. We recommend private hosted zone per environment: staging/prod, and then Route53 inbound endpoints if you need cross-account resolution. For on-prem your DNS team can forward to the VPC resolver. There can be gotchas with search domains and stub resolvers.
[01:48] Ethan: For NAT vs PrivateLink — NAT is simpler for us cause we already have egress, but NAT sends traffic out and back which worries us for audit and also adds extra latency. How big is that latency delta?
[01:59] Priya: In our benchmarks we've seen NAT hairpin adding ~7-20ms median depending on region and NAT gateway type; PrivateLink tends to shave that and gives more predictable tail. But the bigger perf factor for inference is the runtime scheduling and KV cache locality.
[02:17] Liam: To expand—if you use PrivateLink to reach a hosted Redwood control plane and dataplane in our private tenant, the KV cache lives on the inference nodes. If the inference nodes are in the same AZ as your interface endpoint, your cache hits are low-latency. If cross-AZ or cross-account routing occurs you may see 10s of ms increase on cold-hits.
[02:38] Maya: Cold hits meaning first token generation when KV isn't warm?
[02:41] Priya: Exactly. cold KV misses require fetching or recomputing some state leading to higher first-token latency. Our runtime does async prefetching for common prefixes but workload dependent.
[02:52] Ethan: How about batching—if we put requests through PrivateLink and have per-AZ endpoints, will batching be less efficient because traffic is fragmented?
[02:59] Priya: Good question. Batching efficiency depends on request arrival distribution. If you have multiple AZs with shallow qps per AZ, you might see smaller batch sizes per worker. We provide a couple levers: cross-AZ batching via the routing mesh (adds a bit of network hop) or edge-side pooling where frontends buffer briefly to aggregate. Both tradeoffs: increased throughput vs slightly higher P99.
[03:22] Jordan: Also worth noting, quantization choices affect memory and compute. 4-bit quant helps reduce memory and increases throughput on some kernels, but may add a tiny quality delta. For constrained GPU memory (or CPU in some on-prem cases) quantization can prevent KV spilling out to disk which would be catastrophic for latency.
[03:40] Sofia: On compliance — how do audit logs look for PrivateLink flows? we need header-level tracing and token-level cost breakdowns for billing internal teams.
[03:48] Jordan: We emit structured audit logs in JSON with request_id, model, token counts, latency breakdown (frontend, runtime, kv_lookup, kernel). For Private deployments we can deliver logs to S3 or push to your syslog via a connector; KMS can be used for envelope encryption and we support customer-managed keys (CMK).
[04:06] Sofia: And SSO? we use SAML with SCIM provisioning.
[04:09] Jordan: Yes, SSO is supported. For private control plane we integrate with SAML/SSO and can map RBAC groups.
[04:16] Ethan: Back to network specifics — does PrivateLink require one interface endpoint per AZ?
[04:21] Priya: For HA yes, best practice is one per AZ to avoid cross-AZ traffic. Each endpoint gets an ENI and associated IPs, and you need route tables/security groups to allow flows. Also make sure ENI quotas are OK.
[04:34] Liam: Also note NAT vs PrivateLink cost calculus: NAT gateway charges per GB egress, PrivateLink charges per hour per endpoint and per GB. For high QPS low egress size PrivateLink can be cheaper and lower latency; for high outgoing bandwidth NAT can be cheaper but higher latency. We'll share a TCO sheet.
[04:58] Maya: About cross-AZ batching: our app is multi-AZ and we can't afford single-AZ dependencies. You mentioned a routing mesh; is that inside Redwood or an AWS-level thing?
[05:08] Priya: It's inside Redwood's control plane — we can route requests to a warm worker pool across AZs. That incurs an extra hop inside the backbone but helps batch consolidation. We can tune per-route SLOs so latency-sensitive routes avoid cross-AZ aggregation.
[05:23] Ethan: Are there recommended connection timeouts / TCP keepalive settings? we saw connection churn hurt performance in earlier services.
[05:29] Priya: Keep connections warm; we recommend long-lived HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 pooled connections, idle timeout 300s+, and TCP keepalive enabled. Also configure your proxy to allow connection reuse; the runtime supports multiplexing.
[05:44] Maya: On memory footprint — if we run on-prem, what's the typical KV cache size for a 128-token context model?
[05:51] Liam: Depends on model and tokenization. For a 70B-like model with 128 context, KV cache per request can be modest, but aggregated caches per worker can be multiple GBs. If you quantize weights and use 4-bit KV cache packing, we see significant reductions. We'll provide a table for your model.
[06:10] Ethan: We plan to keep everything in private subnet with no public IPs. If we do PrivateLink, do we need NAT at all?
[06:16] Priya: Not necessarily for egress to Redwood if you use PrivateLink for inference and specific control endpoints. But you might still need NAT for ancillary services (package repos, OS updates) unless you use VPC endpoints for those AWS services.
[06:29] Jordan: Quick interjection — for benchmarks we'll instrument per-hop timing so we can show the effect of NAT vs PrivateLink on P50/P95/P99. Priya will run a matrix: single-AZ, multi-AZ with cross-AZ batching, PrivateLink vs NAT.
[06:44] Priya: I'll also include runtime knobs — batch timeout (ms), max batch size, kv cache TTL, quantization profile — and show cost/latency curves.
[06:53] Maya: Security question — is there any traffic that still goes to public internet for model downloads, or can we seed models into a private registry?
[06:59] Liam: We can push model artifacts to S3 in your account or an ECR-like private registry. For air-gapped we support on-prem model packaging. No model downloads over public internet required.
[07:14] Ethan: For DNS resolution — we have split-horizon via Route53 private hosted zones. Does Redwood recommend the AWS resolver 169.254.169.253 style or forwarding to Route53 inbound endpoints?
[07:24] Priya: Use VPC DNS resolver (the .2 IP for AWS) and configure conditional forwarding to Route53 inbound if you need cross-account. For on-prem you can use an inbound Route53 endpoint and forward from your internal DNS. Watch out for TTLs and negative caching when doing service discovery for interface endpoints.
[07:44] Sofia: About encryption — will keys be in our KMS or Redwood's? we need CMK control.
[07:50] Jordan: Customer-managed keys are supported. For private deployments you can hold the KMS keys in your account and we integrate via grants and envelope encryption. For HSM-level controls we have partners that can manage HSM-backed keys if required.
[08:03] Maya: Great. Let's talk about failure modes: if an AZ loses connectivity, do requests route to other AZs automatically?
[08:10] Priya: With PrivateLink and per-AZ endpoints, if an AZ drops you lose that endpoint, but our control plane will route to other healthy endpoints. Cross-AZ routing increases latency but preserves availability. We'll instrument failover and can do a simulated AZ outage during POC.
[08:26] Ethan: What about connection limits on interface endpoints? we have high concurrency bursts and worried about ENI saturation.
[08:32] Liam: ENI quotas and per-endpoint bandwidth are real constraints. We advise sharding endpoints and increasing ENI quotas ahead of peaks. Also enable connection pooling on your side to avoid ephemeral connection explosion.
[08:46] Maya: Let's drill into runtime micro-metrics — you said audit logs include kv_lookup times. can you show an example?
[08:52] Jordan: Sure, sample log line: {request_id: "abc123", model: "redwood-13b-q4", tokens_in: 32, tokens_out: 120, timings: {frontend_ms: 5, runtime_ms: 48, kv_lookup_ms: 12, kernel_ms: 36}} — transcriber note: JSON in transcript may be garbled in export.
[09:09] Priya: For benching we'll produce a CSV with columns per-request for these fields. We'll also attach a flame chart for kernel time vs kv vs batching.
[09:20] Ethan: Regarding quantization — if we go 4-bit we gain memory but what's the P99 impact on model output time?
[09:26] Liam: On some GPUs 4-bit kernels are optimized and actually faster; on older hardware there can be dequant/pack overhead. Expect small variance — we'll include hardware-specific kernels in the report.
[09:40] Maya: For the POC, we want to validate: 1) 95th < 250ms for our 128 token prompt, 2) cost per 1k tokens within our budget, and 3) audit + SSO validated. Does that map to what you can do?
[09:52] Jordan: Yes — we'll structure the POC acceptance criteria to those three. We'll run latency runs and cost estimates.
[09:58] Sofia: On logs delivery — do you push logs into our S3 or does Redwood host them? we want to retain 7 years for compliance.
[10:05] Jordan: We can either push to your S3 (preferred for retention) or stream to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose. Retention handled by your lifecycle policies. We'll provide sample ACLs and encryption configs.
[10:18] Priya: One more networking nuance — if you have corporate proxies that intercept TLS, PrivateLink avoids that because traffic stays inside the VPC. If your proxy is required for egress you'll need to whitelist interface endpoint IPs or run the proxy inside the VPC.
[10:33] Ethan: We do have a transparent proxy for some egress. We need to talk to networking.
[10:36] Maya: Can you also show us a sample terraform for setting up interface endpoints, Route53 zone, and security groups?
[10:42] Priya: Yes — we'll include a terraform sample and a step-by-step. We'll also annotate the security group rules: allow TCP 443 from your app subnets to the endpoint ENI, restrict source ports, and tag ENIs for auditing.
[10:56] Jordan: Let's call out known pitfalls: 1) forgetting to allow the SG <-> ENI flows, 2) ENI quota limits, 3) DNS not resolving to the interface endpoint if private hosted zone not attached to VPC.
[11:07] Ethan: For the bench, what workload generator do you use? we'd like reproducible scripts.
[11:11] Priya: We'll provide a harness based on wrk and a custom client that simulates token streaming and concurrency. We'll share it as a repo link in the doc.
[11:21] Maya: Any limitations for on-prem GPUs? we have a cluster with NVIDIA A100s behind our firewall.
[11:28] Liam: On-prem is supported; you can deploy our private runtime with your kube cluster or via an appliance. Network-wise you still want low-latency connectivity between your app and the runtime; colocating on the same network segment reduces P99. Quantization choices again help fit larger models into the same GPU memory.
[11:45] Sofia: Can we get a diagram of what audit logs look like when encrypted and pushed to S3 (field names, redaction options)?
[11:50] Jordan: Yes, we'll provide schema and redaction knobs. You can redact user PII fields; we recommend token counts and hashes instead of raw prompts for compliance.
[11:59] Priya: Ok quick recap of technical asks: Ethan to send VPC CIDRs and list of subnets, Priya to send PrivateLink vs NAT TCO + terraform snippets, Priya to run bench matrix, Jordan to share security pack.
[12:12] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:16] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench run and a POC plan.
[12:20] (call ends)
